To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

LiCl treatment of Paramecium causes chemoresponse to folate, lactate, and acetate to become repulsive or no response, and that the effect of LiCl is mediated by a mechanism that involves Ca2+ homeostasis.

Li+ inhibits the response of Paramecia to folate, lactate, and acetate, but not to NH4Cl; Li+ treatment slows swimming speed, which is recovered upon incubation in Na+ or K+; and Li+ inhibits Ca efflux from Paramecia, which may be related to the mechanism by how Li+ affects chemoresponse.
(i) LiCl treatment of Paramecium alters the response of the cells to folate, lactate, acetate and cAMP but not to NH4Cl.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which paramecia sense environmental stimuli and respond by altering swimming behavior.
the mechanism of chemoresponse in Parameciamulticellularity and the relationship of the chemoresponse to intracellular ion homeostasis.
the mechanism(s) of chemosensory behavior and its relationship to the regulation of intracellular ions, particularly Li+ and Ca2+.

lithium ions affect the chemoresponse in Paramecimia by perturbing calcium homeostasis.
the Li+ ion is a potent inhibitor of chemoresponse in Paramecim.

Li+ perturbing chemoresponse and swimming behavior may be due to the inhibition of Ca2+ transport.

The main takeaway from our work is that
Li+ is taken up by paramecia, perturbs cholinergic and Ca2+ homeostasis and alters chemotaxis.
Li+ affects chemoresponse by altering the rate of intracellular Ca2+ effflux, which is in turn affected by the presence of Na+ and K+.
the response to Li+ in Paramecia is similar to the effect of Li+ in mammalian neurons and may provide a model to study the mechanisms of action of Li+ in vivo.
